findings.what: The one sentence rewritten this round replaces a false claim with a differently false one, in the same cell and the same defect class. It now says: "The round-5 and round-6 reviewers each re-examined the split and rejected it, the last measuring that none of its own findings touched a scanner." (a) ROUND 6 NEVER CONSIDERED THE SPLIT. Measured: `grep -il 'spl[ai]t' .harness/review/97bfe82bb43e*.json` returns nothing -- neither the round-6 reviewer (4 findings: backlog.md x2, baselines/review.txt, scripts/java_tests.py:391) nor the round-6 test-reviewer (1 finding, RenameFollowingBoundsTest.java:54) mentions splitting, rule 12, or the round cap anywhere. Nor does either record contain any measurement of where its own findings landed. (b) The two reviewers who DID consider and reject the split are ROUND 5's PAIR, f5cfe1cec507: its reviewer's minor on baselines/review.txt ("its central claim that a split would separate `reads()` from the two call sites that make it correct is true of this diff") and its test-reviewer's major ("Remedy is one added fixture, not a split"). That is precisely what the round-7 reviewer wrote in the finding this sentence exists to answer -- the rewrite read "two reviewers" and re-derived them as rounds 5 and 6 rather than as round 5's two roles. (c) The trailing clause is kept verbatim from the draft round 7 called inaccurate in detail: round 5's test-reviewer's second finding IS on a scanner (scripts/test_integrity.py:101, the `sources` predicate), and round 6's reviewer's third finding is on scripts/java_tests.py:391, the shared parser both scanners call. The supportable statement is that neither round found a scanner DEFECT, which is not what the row says. Everything else in the rewritten sentence checks out: the round-4 reviewer (c065ee7a5c22, major on scripts/test_integrity.py:78) did apply rule 12 and did ask for "SPLIT ... or the cap argued with a staged `rounds:M0.53` line", and the staged baselines/review.txt carries that line.
findings.failure_scenario: The cell is the durable record of why a seven-round commit was allowed past a cap of two, and `.harness/review/` is gitignored so nothing downstream can check it. A milestone review, or the next task that wants to argue a `rounds:` entry, reads that TWO INDEPENDENT ROUNDS re-examined the split and rejected it and treats that as two separate confirmations of the argued entry -- when the record shows one round's two roles, and the round the row credits (6) never looked at the question at all. Concretely: the next author facing a round-4-style split demand cites M0.53 as precedent that "later rounds keep re-validating the no-split call", a pattern the record does not contain. It also re-ships the exact clause round 7 blocked on: a reader who does have `.harness/` open sees round 6's minor sitting on scripts/java_tests.py:391 and round 5's test-reviewer minor on scripts/test_integrity.py:101, concludes the row is unreliable, and discounts the parts of it that are true -- including the two measured weakenings relative to HEAD, which are the only content in the cell that a future author must not lose.

findings.what: The cell's closing clause -- "`.harness/review/` is gitignored, so this row is the only surviving account and a wrong one cannot be checked against anything" -- is contradicted by the same commit. `baselines/review.txt`'s staged `rounds:M0.53` entry is a second surviving, in-tree account of the same review history, and it independently records the round-4 split proposal ("The round-4 reviewer proposed three commits (rename-following / tier departure / package re-qualification); the round-5 reviewer, having measured the second weakening, disagreed and said so"). The round-7 reviewer used exactly that entry to falsify the row's previous draft, so a wrong row demonstrably CAN be checked against something.
findings.failure_scenario: A later reader trusting "the only surviving account" edits or deletes one of the two artifacts believing it is the sole copy, and the two prose records of this task's review history drift apart -- which is how the round-7 contradiction (row said no reviewer applied rule 12, baselines entry said a round-4 reviewer proposed three commits) arose in the first place. Recorded rather than blocking, and per review.md rule 11 it is probably better left than fixed, since the fix's own prose becomes round 9's surface.
